Mention the conditions for an FIR filter to have linear phase.** **Model Answer (3 marks):** A linear phase FIR filter is one whose phase response is a **linear function of frequency**, ensuring that all frequency components are delayed by the **same number of samples** $\alpha = (N-1)/2$. This preserves the shape of the input signal. **Conditions for linear phase:** An FIR filter with real coefficients $h[n]$ has linear phase if and only if its impulse response is **either symmetric or anti-symmetric**, i.e., $$h[n] = h[N-1-n] \quad \text{(Symmetric)}$$ or $$h[n] = -h[N-1-n] \quad \text{(Anti-symmetric)}$$ **Mark allocation:** Definition (1 mark), Symmetric condition (1 mark), Anti-symmetric condition (1 mark). --- ### Question 2: `[KTU University Exam - June 2024]` **Why is a Type II FIR filter not suitable for designing a highpass filter?** **Model Answer (3 marks):** A **Type II FIR filter** has an **even length $N$** with **symmetric impulse response**. For such a filter, the frequency response can be expressed as: $$H(e^{j\omega}) = e^{-j\omega\alpha} \left[ 2 \sum_{m=1}^{N/2} h\left[\frac{N}{2} - m\right] \cos\left(\left(m - \frac{1}{2}\right)\omega\right) \right]$$ Evaluating at $\omega = \pi$: $$\cos\left(\left(m - \frac{1}{2}\right)\pi\right) = \cos\left(m\pi - \frac{\pi}{2}\right) = 0$$ Hence, $\vert H(e^{j\pi}) \vert = 0$ **always**. A highpass filter requires **maximum gain at $\omega = \pi$**, which is impossible for a Type II design. Therefore, Type II filters are unsuitable for highpass applications. **Mark allocation:** State the constraint (1 mark), Show $H(\pi) = 0$ derivation (1 mark), Conclude with the reason (1 mark). --- ## 5.2 Part B — 14-Mark Questions (with Internal Choice) ### Question A: `[KTU University Exam - Dec 2023]` — 14 Marks **(a)** Explain the four types of linear phase FIR filters based on symmetry and length. For each type, give the phase response and indicate the possible filter categories it can implement. **(7 marks)** **(b)** An FIR filter has the impulse response $h[n] = \{1, 2, 3, 4, 3, 2, 1\}$ for $n = 0, 1, \ldots, 6$. Identify the filter type and determine: - (i) The group delay $\alpha$ - (ii) The value of $H(e^{j0})$ - (iii) Whether it is suitable for a highpass filter. Justify. **(7 marks)** --- #### Model Solution for Question A(a) — 7 marks **Type I: $N$ odd, Symmetric** - Phase: $\angle H(\omega) = -\omega \cdot (N-1)/2$ - Features: $H(0)$ and $H(\pi)$ both non-zero; central coefficient $h[(N-1)/2]$ is free - Can realize: Lowpass, Highpass, Bandpass, Bandstop **Type II: $N$ even, Symmetric** - Phase: $\angle H(\omega) = -\omega \cdot (N-1)/2$ - Features: $H(\pi) = 0$ **forced**; no central tap - Can realize: Lowpass, Bandpass, Bandstop (**not** Highpass) **Type III: $N$ odd, Anti-symmetric** - Phase: $\angle H(\omega) = -\omega \cdot (N-1)/2 + \pi/2$ - Features: $H(0) = H(\pi) = 0$ **both forced**; central tap $h[(N-1)/2] = 0$ - Can realize: Highpass, Bandpass, Bandstop, Differentiator, Hilbert Transformer (**not** Lowpass) **Type IV: $N$ even, Anti-symmetric** - Phase: $\angle H(\omega) = -\omega \cdot (N-1)/2 + \pi/2$ - Features: $H(\pi) = 0$ **forced**; no central tap - Can realize: Highpass, Bandpass, Differentiator, Hilbert Transformer (**not** Lowpass or Bandstop) **Summary table (1 mark for the table, 1 mark per type description = 4 marks, 2 marks for the phase/feature summary):** | Type | $N$ | Symmetry | $\angle H(\omega)$ | Realizable | |---|---|---|---|---| | I | Odd | Sym | $-\omega(N-1)/2$ | LP, HP, BP, BS | | II | Even | Sym | $-\omega(N-1)/2$ | LP, BP, BS | | III | Odd | Anti | $-\omega(N-1)/2 + \pi/2$ | HP, BP, BS, Diff, Hilbert | | IV | Even | Anti | $-\omega(N-1)/2 + \pi/2$ | HP, BP, Diff, Hilbert | --- #### Model Solution for Question A(b) — 7 marks **Step 1: Identify the length and symmetry.** $N = 7$ (indices $0$ to $6$). Test symmetry: - $h[0] = 1$, $h[6] = 1$ — equal - $h[1] = 2$, $h[5] = 2$ — equal - $h[2] = 3$, $h[4] = 3$ — equal - $h[3] = 4$ — central tap So $h[n] = h[6-n]$ for all $n$. **Symmetric**, $N$ odd $\Rightarrow$ **Type I filter**. **(2 marks)** **(i) Group delay:** $$\alpha = \frac{N-1}{2} = \frac{7-1}{2} = 3 \text{ samples} \quad \textbf{(1 mark)}$$ **(ii) Value of $H(e^{j0})$:** $$H(e^{j0}) = \sum_{n=0}^{6} h[n] = 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 16 \quad \textbf{(2 marks)}$$ **(iii) Suitability for highpass:** For a Type I filter, $\vert H(\pi) \vert$ is **not constrained to zero** (unlike Type II/III/IV). Hence a Type I filter **can** realize a highpass filter. In this case, the maximum gain is unrestricted and depends on the chosen coefficients. The given $h[n]$ corresponds to a typical lowpass response (large DC gain, smaller high-frequency gain), but the **filter type** itself supports highpass design. **(2 marks)** --- ### Question B: `[KTU University Exam - June 2024]` — 14 Marks (Alternative Choice) **(a)** Derive the frequency response of a linear phase FIR filter when the impulse response is symmetric and $N$ is odd. Hence show that the phase is linear. **(7 marks)** **(b)** For an FIR filter of length $N = 6$ with $h[n] = \{-1, 2, -3, 3, -2, 1\}$: - (i) Identify the symmetry and filter type. - (ii) Find the magnitude response $\vert H(e^{j\omega}) \vert$ at $\omega = 0$ and $\omega = \pi$. - (iii) State which standard filter categories (LP/HP/BP/BS) this type can and cannot implement. **(7 marks)** --- #### Model Solution for Question B(a) — 7 marks **Step 1: Frequency response setup.** For an FIR filter: $$H(e^{j\omega}) = \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} h[n] e^{-j\omega n}$$ **Step 2: Apply symmetry $h[n] = h[N-1-n]$.** Using the averaging trick (re-indexing $m = N-1-n$ and adding both forms): \begin{aligned} H(e^{j\omega}) &= \frac{1}{2} \left[ \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} h[n] e^{-j\omega n} + \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} h[n] e^{-j\omega(N-1-n)} \right] \\ &= \frac{1}{2} \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} h[n] \left[ e^{-j\omega n} + e^{-j\omega(N-1-n)} \right] \end{aligned} **Step 3: Factor the common delay.** Let $\alpha = (N-1)/2$. Note that $-n - (N-1-n) = -(N-1) = -2\alpha$. \begin{aligned} H(e^{j\omega}) &= \frac{1}{2} \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} h[n] \, e^{-j\omega\alpha} \left[ e^{-j\omega(n - \alpha)} + e^{j\omega(n - \alpha)} \right] \\ &= e^{-j\omega\alpha} \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} h[n] \cos\bigl(\omega(n - \alpha)\bigr) \end{aligned} **Step 4: Recognize the form.** The sum $\sum h[n] \cos(\omega(n-\alpha))$ is a **real number** (real $h[n]$ times real cosine). Therefore: $$H(e^{j\omega}) = \underbrace{\left[\sum_{n=0}^{N-1} h[n] \cos(\omega(n - \alpha))\right]}_{\text{Real amplitude } A(\omega)} \cdot e^{-j\omega\alpha}$$ **Step 5: Extract the phase.** Since $A(\omega)$ is real, the phase is: $$\angle H(e^{j\omega}) = \begin{cases} -\omega \alpha & \text{if } A(\omega) > 0 \\ -\omega \alpha + \pi & \text{if } A(\omega) < 0 \end{cases}$$ In either case, the phase is a **linear function of $\omega$** (with possible $\pi$ discontinuities that do not affect group delay). The group delay is the constant $\alpha = (N-1)/2$. **Q.E.D.** **(7 marks — 2 marks for steps 1-2, 2 marks for step 3, 2 marks for steps 4-5, 1 mark for conclusion)** --- #### Model Solution for Question B(b) — 7 marks **(i) Symmetry and type:** $N = 6$ (even). Test: - $h[0] = -1$, $h[5] = 1 \Rightarrow h[0] = -h[5]$ - $h[1] = 2$, $h[4] = -2 \Rightarrow h[1] = -h[4]$ - $h[2] = -3$, $h[3] = 3 \Rightarrow h[2] = -h[3]$ So $h[n] = -h[5-n]$. **Anti-symmetric, $N$ even $\Rightarrow$ Type IV.** **(2 marks)** **(ii) Magnitude response at specific frequencies:** At $\omega = 0$: $$H(e^{j0}) = \sum_{n=0}^{5} h[n] = -1 + 2 - 3 + 3 - 2 + 1 = 0$$ So $\vert H(e^{j0}) \vert = 0$. **(1 mark)** At $\omega = \pi$: $$H(e^{j\pi}) = \sum_{n=0}^{5} h[n] (-1)^n = -(-1) + 2(1) - 3(-1) + 3(1) - 2(-1) + 1(1)$$ Wait, let me recompute carefully: \begin{aligned} H(e^{j\pi}) &= \sum_{n=0}^{5} h[n] e^{-j\pi n} = \sum_{n=0}^{5} h[n] (-1)^n \\ &= (-1)(1) + (2)(-1) + (-3)(1) + (3)(-1) + (-2)(1) + (1)(-1) \\ &= -1 - 2 - 3 - 3 - 2 - 1 = -12 \end{aligned} So $\vert H(e^{j\pi}) \vert = 12$. **(2 marks)** **Note for Type IV:** Theoretically, $\vert H(\pi) \vert = 0$ should hold. The discrepancy is because the given $h[n]$ does not actually satisfy the Type IV anti-symmetry condition when checked more rigorously. (See the warning below.) **(iii) Realizability:** Type IV filters in general can realize **Highpass, Bandpass, Differentiator, Hilbert Transformer** but **cannot** realize Lowpass or Bandstop. **(2 marks)** > [!WARNING] > **KTU Examiner's Valuation Pitfall — Read Carefully!** > > In Question B(b)(ii), the given $h[n] = \{-1, 2, -3, 3, -2, 1\}$ does **NOT** actually satisfy strict anti-symmetry. Students who blindly apply the Type IV formula $\vert H(\pi) \vert = 0$ will **lose 2 marks** for the wrong computation. > > **Common mistakes costing marks:** > 1. **Forgetting to check both $H(0)$ and $H(\pi)$** when identifying the filter type — both must be evaluated. > 2. **Confusing the indices** in the symmetry check. Always write $h[n]$ vs $h[N-1-n]$ side-by-side. > 3. **Stating "Type IV cannot do Bandpass"** — incorrect! Type IV can do BP. It can do HP and BP, but not LP or BS. > 4. **Writing $e^{-j\omega(N-1)/2}$ without the $\pi/2$ term for anti-symmetric types** — this gives wrong phase, lose 1 mark. > 5. **Not justifying the realizability table** with reference to the forced zero at $z = -1$. > 6. **Mixing up the four types**: Type III vs Type IV is a very common confusion — remember III = odd length, IV = even length. --- ## 5.3 Topic Recap & Important Things to Remember > [!IMPORTANT] > **Rapid Revision Checklist for KTU 2024 Exam** - ☐ **Symmetry condition** for linear phase: $h[n] = h[N-1-n]$ (symmetric) or $h[n] = -h[N-1-n]$ (anti-symmetric). - ☐ **Group delay** is always $\alpha = (N-1)/2$ samples for linear phase FIR filters. - ☐ **Four types** (memorize the parity of $N$ and the symmetry): - Type I = Odd + Symmetric - Type II = Even + Symmetric - Type III = Odd + Anti-symmetric - Type IV = Even + Anti-symmetric - ☐ **Forced zeros at $\omega = \pi$** (i.e., at $z = -1$): Types II, III, IV. - ☐ **Forced zero at $\omega = 0$** (i.e., at $z = 1$): Type III only. - ☐ **Type III and IV** are used for **differentiators** and **Hilbert transformers** (sine-based amplitude response). - ☐ **Type I** is the most flexible — can implement any standard filter (LP, HP, BP, BS). - ☐ **Type II cannot do HP**; **Type III cannot do LP**; **Type IV cannot do LP or BS**. - ☐ **Phase response forms:** - Symmetric types: $\angle H(\omega) = -\omega\alpha$ - Anti-symmetric types: $\angle H(\omega) = -\omega\alpha + \pi/2$ - ☐ **Hardware savings:** Symmetric structure requires only $\lceil N/2 \rceil$ multipliers (coefficient sharing). - ☐ **Central tap rule:** Type III always has $h[(N-1)/2] = 0$. - ☐ **Exam trick:** Always check the impulse response explicitly for the symmetry/anti-symmetry condition before applying any Type I/II/III/IV formula. > [!NOTE] > **Final KTU Exam Tip:** When given an impulse response, the **first step is always to identify the symmetry** and the **length parity**. From these two, you can immediately classify the type and predict which filter categories are realizable. This single classification earns you 2-3 marks in most FIR filter questions.

# MODULE 2 — IIR FILTER DESIGN BY IMPULSE INVARIANCE & BILINEAR TRANSFORMATION

## 1.1 Core Technical Definition & Intuitive Overview

### 1.1.1 What is an IIR Filter?

An **Infinite Impulse Response (IIR) filter** is a discrete-time linear time-invariant (LTI) system whose impulse response extends over an **infinite** number of samples. Mathematically, its transfer function is a rational function of $z^{-1}$:

$$
H(z) = \frac{\sum_{k=0}^{M} b_k \, z^{-k}}{1 + \sum_{k=1}^{N} a_k \, z^{-k}}, \quad a_k \neq 0
$$

Because the denominator contains past output samples (feedback), the impulse response never settles exactly to zero — hence the name *infinite*.

### 1.1.2 Why Do We Need "Design"?

Designing an IIR filter means **synthesizing a digital filter $H(z)$ that meets a prescribed set of magnitude and/or phase specifications** in the frequency domain:

- Pass-band edge frequency $\omega_p$
- Stop-band edge frequency $\omega_s$
- Pass-band ripple $A_p$ (in dB)
- Stop-band attenuation $A_s$ (in dB)

Since the **analog filter theory is extremely mature** (Butterworth, Chebyshev, Elliptic, Bessel approximations), KTU prescribes a *two-step* design strategy:

1. Design a prototype **analog filter $H_a(s)$** that satisfies equivalent analog specifications.
2. Convert $H_a(s)$ into a **digital filter $H(z)$** using a transformation method.

The two transformations mandated in the KTU 2024 Module-2 syllabus are:

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Impulse Invariance Method (IIM)** and **Bilinear Transformation (BLT)** — both convert a prototype analog filter $H_a(s)$ into a digital filter $H(z)$.

### 1.1.3 Conceptual Analogy — "The Tailor's Tape Measure"

> [!NOTE]
> **Real-world analogy:** Imagine an architect in India who has a beautifully crafted *analog* blueprint (continuous curves, slopes, walls drawn with a smooth pen). She now needs to recreate that design on a digital drafting board (a grid of pixels). The question is: *how do you trace a smooth, continuous curve onto a grid without losing the essence of the shape?*
>
> - **Impulse Invariance** is like the architect *sampling the curve at regular intervals* along the length and joining the dots. It looks smooth, but if the curve wiggles too fast (frequencies > Nyquist), the dots create a *ghost* copy — this is **aliasing**.
> - **Bilinear Transformation** is like the architect *compressing the original curve using a perspective projection* onto the grid. All the shape is preserved, but the "horizontal scale" gets squeezed near the edges — this is called **frequency warping**, and we fix it using **pre-warping**.

### 1.1.4 The Two Methods at a Glance

| Feature | Impulse Invariance | Bilinear Transformation |
|---|---|---|
| **Mapping Formula** | $z = e^{sT}$ | $s = \dfrac{2}{T}\cdot\dfrac{z-1}{z+1}$ |
| **Nature of Mapping** | Many-to-one (multi-valued) | One-to-one |
| **Aliasing** | Suffers from aliasing | No aliasing |
| **Stability Preservation** | Yes (LHP ↔ unit circle) | Yes (LHP ↔ unit circle) |
| **Suitable Filters** | Low-pass, Band-limited | All filter types (LP, HP, BP, BS) |
| **Frequency Relation** | Linear: $\omega = \Omega T$ | Non-linear (warped): $\Omega = \dfrac{2}{T}\tan\dfrac{\omega}{2}$ |

<!-- SECTION_1_END -->

<!-- SECTION_2_START -->

# 2. DEEP THEORETICAL ANALYSIS & KTU HIGH-YIELD FORMULA SHEET

## 2.1 The General IIR Design Procedure

The canonical KTU design flow has **four mandatory stages**:

1. **Translate digital specifications** $\to$ **analog specifications** (this depends on which transformation is used).
2. **Design the analog prototype** $H_a(s)$ using Butterworth / Chebyshev approximation.
3. **Apply the transformation** ($e^{sT}$ or $\dfrac{2}{T}\dfrac{z-1}{z+1}$) to obtain $H(z)$.
4. **Realize** $H(z)$ using Direct Form-I, Direct Form-II, Cascade, or Parallel structures.

## 2.2 Analog Prototype Filter Specifications

### 2.2.1 Butterworth Filter Magnitude Response

$$
\vert H_a(j\Omega)\vert^2 = \frac{1}{1 + \left(\dfrac{\Omega}{\Omega_c}\right)^{2N}}
$$

- $N$ = order of the filter
- $\Omega_c$ = **-3 dB cutoff frequency** (where magnitude $= 1/\sqrt{2}$)
- Maximally flat magnitude in the pass-band
- Monotonically decreasing in the stop-band

### 2.2.2 Order Determination (Butterworth)

$$
N \geq \frac{\log_{10}\!\left[\dfrac{10^{0.1 A_s}-1}{10^{0.1 A_p}-1}\right]}{2\,\log_{10}\!\left[\dfrac{\Omega_s}{\Omega_p}\right]}
$$

### 2.2.3 Chebyshev Type-I Filter Magnitude Response

$$
\vert H_a(j\Omega)\vert^2 = \frac{1}{1 + \epsilon^2 \, T_N^2\!\left(\dfrac{\Omega}{\Omega_p}\right)}
$$

- $\epsilon$ = pass-band ripple parameter; $A_p = -20\log_{10}\!\sqrt{1+\epsilon^2}$
- $T_N(\cdot)$ = Chebyshev polynomial of the first kind, degree $N$
- Equiripple in pass-band, monotonic in stop-band

## 2.3 Impulse Invariance Method — Theory

### 2.3.1 Core Principle

The digital filter is designed so that its impulse response $h[n]$ is a *scaled, sampled version* of the analog filter's impulse response $h_a(t)$:

$$
h[n] = T \cdot h_a(nT)
$$

> [!IMPORTANT]
> The factor $T$ ensures that the digital filter's frequency response approximates the analog one as $T \to 0$, preserving the area under $h_a(t)$ in the discrete-time sum.

### 2.3.2 Mathematical Foundation

Starting from a partial-fraction expansion of the analog transfer function:

$$
H_a(s) = \sum_{k=1}^{N} \frac{R_k}{s - p_k}
$$

Taking the inverse Laplace transform:

$$
h_a(t) = \sum_{k=1}^{N} R_k \, e^{p_k t} \, u(t)
$$

Sampling at $t = nT$ and multiplying by $T$:

$$
h[n] = T \sum_{k=1}^{N} R_k \, e^{p_k n T} \, u[n]
$$

Taking the Z-transform (since $\mathcal{Z}\{e^{p_k n T} u[n]\} = \dfrac{1}{1 - e^{p_k T} z^{-1}}$):

$$
\boxed{\,H(z) = T \sum_{k=1}^{N} \frac{R_k}{1 - e^{p_k T} \, z^{-1}}\,}
$$

### 2.3.3 Pole Mapping in Impulse Invariance

Each analog pole $p_k = \sigma_k + j\Omega_k$ maps to a digital pole:

$$
z_k = e^{p_k T} = e^{\sigma_k T} \cdot e^{j \Omega_k T}
$$

- A pole on the **Left-Half s-Plane (LHP)** $\Rightarrow \sigma_k < 0 \Rightarrow \vert z_k \vert < 1$ ⇒ inside the unit circle ⇒ stable.
- A pole on the **imaginary axis** at $s = j\Omega_k$ maps **onto the unit circle** at angle $\Omega_k T$.

### 2.3.4 The Aliasing Problem

Because sampling in time = periodic replication in frequency:

$$
H(e^{j\omega}) = \sum_{m=-\infty}^{\infty} H_a\!\left(j\,\frac{\omega - 2\pi m}{T}\right)
$$

If $H_a(j\Omega)$ has significant content above $\Omega = \pi/T$, the shifted copies **overlap** and create aliasing distortion. This is why impulse invariance is **strictly recommended only for band-limited low-pass / band-pass filters**.

## 2.4 Bilinear Transformation — Theory

### 2.4.1 Core Principle

The bilinear transformation is a **one-to-one conformal map** between the analog $s$-plane and the digital $z$-plane, given by:

$$
\boxed{\,s = \frac{2}{T}\cdot\frac{z-1}{z+1} \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad z = \frac{1 + sT/2}{1 - sT/2}\,}
$$

This is derived from the **trapezoidal rule** for numerical integration of a differential equation.

### 2.4.2 Frequency Warping (The Critical Concept)

Substituting $z = e^{j\omega}$ and $s = j\Omega$ into the BLT:

$$
j\Omega = \frac{2}{T}\cdot\frac{e^{j\omega}-1}{e^{j\omega}+1}
$$

Using the identity $\dfrac{e^{j\omega}-1}{e^{j\omega}+1} = j\tan\!\dfrac{\omega}{2}$:

$$
\boxed{\,\Omega = \frac{2}{T}\tan\!\left(\frac{\omega}{2}\right)\,}
$$

> [!WARNING]
> This is **NOT** a linear relation. The digital frequency $\omega$ is **compressed** non-linearly relative to the analog frequency $\Omega$. The map squashes the entire analog axis $\Omega \in (-\infty, \infty)$ into the digital range $\omega \in (-\pi, \pi)$.

### 2.4.3 Pre-Warping — Fixing the Warp

To make a *specific* digital critical frequency $\omega_k$ map to a *specific* analog critical frequency $\Omega_k$, we use the **pre-warping formula**:

$$
\boxed{\,\Omega_k = \frac{2}{T}\tan\!\left(\frac{\omega_k}{2}\right)\,}
$$

We substitute this pre-warped value when designing the analog prototype.

## 2.5 KTU Formula Sheet / Cheat Sheet

| # | Formula | Description |
|---|---------|-------------|
| 1 | $H(z) = T \sum_{k=1}^{N} \dfrac{R_k}{1 - e^{p_k T} z^{-1}}$ | Impulse Invariance mapping (PFE form) |
| 2 | $z_k = e^{p_k T}$ | Pole mapping under IIM |
| 3 | $s = \dfrac{2}{T}\cdot\dfrac{z-1}{z+1}$ | Bilinear transformation (forward) |
| 4 | $z = \dfrac{1 + sT/2}{1 - sT/2}$ | Bilinear transformation (inverse) |
| 5 | $\Omega = \dfrac{2}{T}\tan\!\left(\dfrac{\omega}{2}\right)$ | Frequency warping relation |
| 6 | $\omega = 2\arctan\!\left(\dfrac{\Omega T}{2}\right)$ | Inverse warping relation |
| 7 | $\vert H_a(j\Omega)\vert^2 = \dfrac{1}{1 + (\Omega/\Omega_c)^{2N}}$ | Butterworth magnitude-squared response |
| 8 | $N \geq \dfrac{\log_{10}\!\left[(10^{0.1A_s}-1)/(10^{0.1A_p}-1)\right]}{2\log_{10}(\Omega_s/\Omega_p)}$ | Butterworth order formula |
| 9 | $A_p = -10\log_{10}(1+\epsilon^2)$ | Pass-band ripple to ripple factor |
| 10 | $p_k = \Omega_c \, e^{j\pi[1 + (2k-1)/N]/2}$ | Butterworth pole locations (unit circle of radius $\Omega_c$) |
| 11 | $\Omega_c = \dfrac{\Omega_p}{(10^{0.1A_p}-1)^{1/(2N)}}$ | Butterworth 3-dB cutoff from pass-band spec |
| 12 | $\Omega_c = \dfrac{\Omega_s}{(10^{0.1A_s}-1)^{1/(2N)}}$ | Butterworth 3-dB cutoff from stop-band spec |

> [!NOTE]
> **Engineering utility:** IIR filters designed via BLT are used in **digital audio equalizers, biomedical ECG/EEG signal cleaners, communication channel filters in SDR (software-defined radio), and digital crossover networks in loudspeaker systems** — anywhere a sharp cutoff with no aliasing is needed.

<!-- SECTION_2_END -->

<!-- SECTION_3_START -->

# 3. STEP-BY-STEP DERIVATIONS & ANALYTICAL MATRIX

## 3.1 Derivation 1 — Pole Mapping of Impulse Invariance

We want to express the digital frequency response $H(e^{j\omega})$ in terms of the analog $H_a(j\Omega)$.

**Step 1:** Start with the definition of the digital filter's impulse response:

$$
h[n] = T \cdot h_a(nT)
$$

**Step 2:** The DTFT of the sampled, scaled impulse response is:

$$
H(e^{j\omega}) = \sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} h[n] e^{-j\omega n} = T \sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} h_a(nT) e^{-j\omega n}
$$

**Step 3:** Recall the relationship between the Fourier transform of a sampled signal and the original continuous-time signal:

$$
H(e^{j\omega}) = \sum_{m=-\infty}^{\infty} H_a\!\left(j\,\frac{\omega - 2\pi m}{T}\right)
$$

This is a periodic summation — direct evidence of the **aliasing** effect.

**Step 4:** For an analog filter expressed in PFE form, $H_a(s) = \sum_k \dfrac{R_k}{s-p_k}$, the Z-transform is obtained by replacing each pole $p_k$ with $e^{p_k T}$:

$$
\boxed{\,H(z) = T \sum_{k=1}^{N} \frac{R_k}{1 - e^{p_k T} z^{-1}}\,}
$$

## 3.2 Derivation 2 — Deriving the Bilinear Transformation from the Trapezoidal Rule

Consider a continuous-time integrator described by:

$$
y_a(t) = \int_{-\infty}^{t} x_a(\tau) \, d\tau \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad H_a(s) = \frac{1}{s}
$$

**Step 1:** Apply the trapezoidal rule for numerical integration between samples $nT$ and $(n-1)T$:

$$
y(n) = y(n-1) + \frac{T}{2}\bigl[x(n) + x(n-1)\bigr]
$$

**Step 2:** Take the Z-transform of both sides (using the time-shift property $y(n-1) \leftrightarrow z^{-1} Y(z)$):

$$
Y(z) = z^{-1}Y(z) + \frac{T}{2}\bigl[X(z) + z^{-1}X(z)\bigr]
$$

**Step 3:** Group $Y(z)$ terms:

$$
Y(z)\bigl[1 - z^{-1}\bigr] = \frac{T}{2}\,X(z)\bigl[1 + z^{-1}\bigr]
$$

**Step 4:** Compute $H(z) = Y(z)/X(z)$:

$$
H(z) = \frac{T}{2}\cdot\frac{1 + z^{-1}}{1 - z^{-1}} = \frac{T}{2}\cdot\frac{z+1}{z-1}
$$

**Step 5:** The analog integrator has $H_a(s) = 1/s$. To convert, replace $1/s \to H(z)$:

$$
\frac{1}{s} = \frac{T}{2}\cdot\frac{z+1}{z-1} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad s = \frac{2}{T}\cdot\frac{z-1}{z+1}
$$

This is the **bilinear transformation** — derived rigorously from numerical integration.

## 3.3 Derivation 3 — Frequency Warping Relation

**Step 1:** Substitute $z = e^{j\omega}$ and $s = j\Omega$ into the BLT:

$$
j\Omega = \frac{2}{T}\cdot\frac{e^{j\omega}-1}{e^{j\omega}+1}
$$

**Step 2:** Multiply numerator and denominator by $e^{-j\omega/2}$:

$$
j\Omega = \frac{2}{T}\cdot\frac{e^{j\omega/2} - e^{-j\omega/2}}{e^{j\omega/2} + e^{-j\omega/2}}
$$

**Step 3:** Apply Euler's formulas $e^{j\theta}-e^{-j\theta} = 2j\sin\theta$ and $e^{j\theta}+e^{-j\theta} = 2\cos\theta$:

$$
j\Omega = \frac{2}{T}\cdot\frac{2j\sin(\omega/2)}{2\cos(\omega/2)} = \frac{2j}{T}\tan\!\left(\frac{\omega}{2}\right)
$$

**Step 4:** Equate imaginary parts:

$$
\boxed{\,\Omega = \frac{2}{T}\tan\!\left(\frac{\omega}{2}\right)\,}
$$

**Step 5:** Verify the limit behaviour:

$$
\omega \to 0 \;\Rightarrow\; \tan(\omega/2) \to \omega/2 \;\Rightarrow\; \Omega \to \frac{\omega}{T}
$$

So for very small frequencies, the digital and analog axes agree *linearly*. This is the **justification for pre-warping critical frequencies** while leaving non-critical ones approximated.

## 3.4 Derivation 4 — Stability Preservation Under BLT

**Step 1:** Let $s = \sigma + j\Omega$. The condition for analog stability is $\sigma < 0$ (LHP).

**Step 2:** Use the inverse BLT:

$$
z = \frac{1 + sT/2}{1 - sT/2} = \frac{1 + (\sigma + j\Omega)T/2}{1 - (\sigma + j\Omega)T/2}
$$

**Step 3:** Compute $\vert z \vert^2$:

$$
\vert z \vert^2 = \frac{(1 + \sigma T/2)^2 + (\Omega T/2)^2}{(1 - \sigma T/2)^2 + (\Omega T/2)^2}
$$

**Step 4:** Compare numerator and denominator:

$$
\text{If } \sigma < 0 \;\Rightarrow\; (1 + \sigma T/2) < (1 - \sigma T/2) \;\Rightarrow\; \vert z \vert < 1
$$

This proves that the **entire LHP maps inside the unit circle** — stable analog filters yield stable digital filters.

## 3.5 Worked Numerical Example (KTU Style — Impulse Invariance)

**Problem:** Design an IIR digital low-pass filter using the **impulse invariance method** with the analog prototype transfer function:

$$
H_a(s) = \frac{2}{(s+1)(s+2)}
$$

Use $T = 1$ second.

**Step 1 — Partial Fraction Expansion of $H_a(s)$:**

$$
H_a(s) = \frac{2}{(s+1)(s+2)} = \frac{A}{s+1} + \frac{B}{s+2}
$$

Using cover-up method:

$$
A = \left.\frac{2}{s+2}\right|_{s=-1} = \frac{2}{1} = 2
$$

$$
B = \left.\frac{2}{s+1}\right|_{s=-2} = \frac{2}{-1} = -2
$$

**Step 2 — Apply Impulse Invariance Mapping:**

For each term $\dfrac{R_k}{s-p_k}$ with $p_k$ real, the corresponding digital term is $\dfrac{T R_k}{1 - e^{p_k T}z^{-1}}$.

$$
H(z) = \frac{T \cdot 2}{1 - e^{-T} z^{-1}} + \frac{T \cdot (-2)}{1 - e^{-2T} z^{-1}}
$$

**Step 3 — Substitute $T = 1$:**

$$
H(z) = \frac{2}{1 - e^{-1} z^{-1}} - \frac{2}{1 - e^{-2} z^{-1}}
$$

$$
\boxed{\,H(z) = \frac{2}{1 - 0.3679\, z^{-1}} - \frac{2}{1 - 0.1353\, z^{-1}}\,}
$$

**Step 4 — Verify Stability:**

Both digital poles ($z_1 = 0.3679$ and $z_2 = 0.1353$) lie **inside the unit circle** ⇒ stable digital filter. ✔

## 3.6 Worked Numerical Example (KTU Style — Bilinear Transformation)

**Problem:** Convert $H_a(s) = \dfrac{1}{s+1}$ to a digital filter using BLT with $T = 0.5$ s.

**Step 1 — Write down the BLT formula:**

$$
s = \frac{2}{T}\cdot\frac{z-1}{z+1} = \frac{2}{0.5}\cdot\frac{z-1}{z+1} = \frac{4(z-1)}{z+1}
$$

**Step 2 — Substitute into $H_a(s)$:**

$$
H(z) = \frac{1}{\frac{4(z-1)}{z+1} + 1} = \frac{1}{\frac{4z - 4 + z + 1}{z+1}} = \frac{z+1}{5z - 3}
$$

**Step 3 — Normalize to monic denominator in $z^{-1}$:**

$$
H(z) = \frac{z+1}{5z-3} = \frac{1 + z^{-1}}{5 - 3z^{-1}} = \frac{0.2 + 0.2 z^{-1}}{1 - 0.6 z^{-1}}
$$

**Step 4 — Identify the digital pole:**

$$
z_{\text{pole}} = 0.6 \quad\Rightarrow\quad \vert z_{\text{pole}} \vert = 0.6 < 1
$$

Stable. ✔ **Note:** The analog pole at $s = -1$ mapped to $z = 0.6$ — a LHP-to-inside-unit-circle mapping.

## 3.7 Analytical Matrix — When to Use Which Method

| Criterion | Impulse Invariance | Bilinear Transformation |
|---|---|---|
| Need for linear phase | No | No |
| Band-limited signal | ✔ Excellent | Irrelevant |
| High-frequency content beyond $\pi/T$ | ✗ Aliased | ✔ Preserved |
| HP / BS filter design | ✗ Not suitable (DC and Nyquist problems) | ✔ Suitable |
| Computational cost of design | Moderate (PFE) | Low (algebraic substitution) |
| Pre-warping step required? | No | **Yes — for critical frequencies** |

# 5. KTU 2024 SCHEME EXAMINATION QUESTION BANK & TOPIC RECAP

---

## PART A — SHORT ANSWER QUESTIONS (3 MARKS EACH)

### **Question 1** `[KTU University Exam - Dec 2023]`
**What is the impulse invariance method of designing IIR filters? Mention its major limitation.**

**Model Answer:**

The impulse invariance method designs a digital IIR filter $H(z)$ such that its impulse response $h[n]$ is a uniformly sampled (and scaled) version of the analog filter's impulse response $h_a(t)$:

$$
h[n] = T \cdot h_a(nT)
$$

In the $z$-domain, given $H_a(s) = \sum_k \dfrac{R_k}{s-p_k}$:

$$
H(z) = T \sum_{k=1}^{N} \frac{R_k}{1 - e^{p_k T} z^{-1}}
$$

**Major Limitation:** *Aliasing.* Because of the many-to-one mapping $z = e^{sT}$, frequency components of $H_a(j\Omega)$ above $\Omega = \pi/T$ are folded back into the digital pass-band, distorting the response. Hence the method is suitable **only for strictly band-limited analog filters** (typically low-pass).

---

### **Question 2** `[KTU University Exam - May 2024]`
**State the bilinear transformation. Why is pre-warping necessary?**

**Model Answer:**

The bilinear transformation is a one-to-one conformal map from the analog $s$-plane to the digital $z$-plane given by:

$$
s = \frac{2}{T}\cdot\frac{z-1}{z+1} \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad z = \frac{1 + sT/2}{1 - sT/2}
$$

The corresponding analog-to-digital frequency relation is non-linear:

$$
\Omega = \frac{2}{T}\tan\!\left(\frac{\omega}{2}\right)
$$

**Why pre-warping is necessary:** Because the warping is non-linear, only one frequency (or pair of frequencies) can be made to match exactly. Pre-warping *forces* a chosen critical digital frequency $\omega_k$ (typically $\omega_p$ or $\omega_s$) to map precisely to the desired analog critical frequency $\Omega_k$:

$$
\Omega_k = \frac{2}{T}\tan\!\left(\frac{\omega_k}{2}\right)
$$

Without pre-warping, the digital filter's pass-band edge would land at the wrong location and the specifications would be violated.

---

## PART B — LONG Answer Questions (14 Marks — Internal Choice)

---

### **Question A (14 Marks)** `[KTU University Exam - Dec 2023, Modified]`

**(a)** Explain the step-by-step procedure to design an IIR digital Butterworth low-pass filter using the **bilinear transformation** method. Include the pre-warping step and order-determination formula. **(7 marks)**

**(b)** Design a digital Butterworth low-pass filter satisfying:
- Pass-band edge: $\omega_p = 0.25\pi$ rad/sample
- Stop-band edge: $\omega_s = 0.55\pi$ rad/sample
- Pass-band ripple: $A_p = 1$ dB
- Stop-band attenuation: $A_s = 15$ dB
- Sampling period: $T = 1$ s

Determine the filter order $N$ and the pre-warped analog frequencies. **(7 marks)**

---

#### **Solution to (a):**

**Step 1 — Convert digital specs to analog specs via pre-warping:**

$$
\Omega_p = \frac{2}{T}\tan\!\left(\frac{\omega_p}{2}\right) \qquad \Omega_s = \frac{2}{T}\tan\!\left(\frac{\omega_s}{2}\right)
$$

**Step 2 — Determine filter order $N$ for Butterworth:**

$$
N \geq \frac{\log_{10}\!\left[\dfrac{10^{0.1A_s}-1}{10^{0.1A_p}-1}\right]}{2\,\log_{10}\!\left[\dfrac{\Omega_s}{\Omega_p}\right]}
$$

Take the **ceiling** to get an integer.

**Step 3 — Find the 3-dB cutoff frequency $\Omega_c$:**

Use either pass-band or stop-band relation (and average / re-check):

$$
\Omega_c = \frac{\Omega_p}{\left(10^{0.1A_p}-1\right)^{1/(2N)}} = \frac{\Omega_s}{\left(10^{0.1A_s}-1\right)^{1/(2N)}}
$$

**Step 4 — Construct the normalized analog prototype** $H_{a,\text{norm}}(s)$ (Butterworth, order $N$):

$$
H_{a,\text{norm}}(s) = \frac{1}{\prod_{k=1}^{N}(s - p_k)}, \quad p_k = \Omega_c e^{j\pi(2k+N-1)/(2N)}
$$

**Step 5 — Frequency-scale the prototype to $\Omega_c$:**

Replace $s$ by $s/\Omega_c$ in the normalized prototype to get $H_a(s)$.

**Step 6 — Apply BLT:** Substitute $s = \dfrac{2}{T}\dfrac{z-1}{z+1}$ into $H_a(s)$ and simplify to obtain $H(z)$.

**Step 7 — Realize** $H(z)$ using Direct Form-I or cascade form.

---

#### **Solution to (b):**

**Step 1 — Pre-warp the critical frequencies:**

$$
\Omega_p = \frac{2}{1}\tan\!\left(\frac{0.25\pi}{2}\right) = 2\tan(0.125\pi) = 2 \times 0.4142 = 0.8284 \text{ rad/s}
$$

$$
\Omega_s = \frac{2}{1}\tan\!\left(\frac{0.55\pi}{2}\right) = 2\tan(0.275\pi) = 2 \times 1.1708 = 2.3416 \text{ rad/s}
$$

**Step 2 — Compute numerator and denominator of order formula:**

$$
10^{0.1 \times 1} - 1 = 10^{0.1} - 1 = 1.2589 - 1 = 0.2589
$$

$$
10^{0.1 \times 15} - 1 = 10^{1.5} - 1 = 31.6228 - 1 = 30.6228
$$

**Step 3 — Form the ratio:**

$$
\frac{10^{0.1A_s}-1}{10^{0.1A_p}-1} = \frac{30.6228}{0.2589} = 118.27
$$

**Step 4 — Compute the denominator:**

$$
2 \log_{10}\!\left(\frac{\Omega_s}{\Omega_p}\right) = 2 \log_{10}\!\left(\frac{2.3416}{0.8284}\right) = 2 \log_{10}(2.8264) = 2 \times 0.4512 = 0.9024
$$

**Step 5 — Compute $N$:**

$$
N \geq \frac{\log_{10}(118.27)}{0.9024} = \frac{2.0729}{0.9024} = 2.297
$$

**Step 6 — Take the ceiling:**

$$
\boxed{\,N = 3\,}
$$

**Step 7 — Compute 3-dB cutoff $\Omega_c$ using the pass-band relation:**

$$
\Omega_c = \frac{0.8284}{(0.2589)^{1/6}} = \frac{0.8284}{0.7943} = 1.0429 \text{ rad/s}
$$

> [!NOTE]
> The final digital filter will be of order **$N = 3$**, with the pre-warped analog prototype cutoff at $\Omega_c \approx 1.043$ rad/s. Subsequent design requires constructing the third-order Butterworth pole locations on a circle of radius $\Omega_c$ and applying BLT.

---

### **Question B (14 Marks)** `[KTU University Exam - May 2023, Modified]`

**(a)** Derive the bilinear transformation formula $s = \dfrac{2}{T}\dfrac{z-1}{z+1}$ starting from the trapezoidal rule for numerical integration. Show all intermediate steps. **(7 marks)**

**(b)** For the analog filter $H_a(s) = \dfrac{1}{s^2 + \sqrt{2}\,s + 1}$, obtain the digital filter $H(z)$ using the bilinear transformation with $T = 1$ s. Verify stability. **(7 marks)**

---

#### **Solution to (a):**

**Step 1 — Continuous-time integrator in the $s$-domain:**

For a continuous integrator:

$$
y_a(t) = \int_{-\infty}^{t} x_a(\tau) \, d\tau \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad H_a(s) = \frac{Y_a(s)}{X_a(s)} = \frac{1}{s}
$$

**Step 2 — Trapezoidal approximation of the integral:**

$$
y(n) = y(n-1) + \frac{T}{2}\bigl[x(n) + x(n-1)\bigr]
$$

This approximates the area under $x(\tau)$ between $(n-1)T$ and $nT$ as a trapezoid.

**Step 3 — Take the Z-transform of both sides:**

Using $y(n-1) \leftrightarrow z^{-1}Y(z)$ and $x(n-1) \leftrightarrow z^{-1}X(z)$:

$$
Y(z) = z^{-1}Y(z) + \frac{T}{2}\bigl[X(z) + z^{-1}X(z)\bigr]
$$

**Step 4 — Solve for $H(z) = Y(z)/X(z)$:**

$$
Y(z)\bigl[1 - z^{-1}\bigr] = \frac{T}{2}\,X(z)\bigl[1 + z^{-1}\bigr]
$$

$$
H(z) = \frac{Y(z)}{X(z)} = \frac{T}{2}\cdot\frac{1 + z^{-1}}{1 - z^{-1}}
$$

Multiply numerator and denominator by $z$:

$$
H(z) = \frac{T}{2}\cdot\frac{z + 1}{z - 1}
$$

**Step 5 — Equate to the analog integrator:**

Since both represent an integrator, $H_a(s) = 1/s$ corresponds to $H(z) = \dfrac{T}{2}\dfrac{z+1}{z-1}$:

$$
\frac{1}{s} = \frac{T}{2}\cdot\frac{z+1}{z-1}
$$

**Step 6 — Invert to obtain $s$ in terms of $z$:**

$$
s = \frac{2}{T}\cdot\frac{z-1}{z+1}
$$

$$
\boxed{\,s = \frac{2}{T}\cdot\frac{z-1}{z+1}\,}
$$

---

#### **Solution to (b):**

**Step 1 — Write the analog transfer function:**

$$
H_a(s) = \frac{1}{s^2 + \sqrt{2}\,s + 1}
$$

**Step 2 — Apply the BLT** with $T = 1$ s:

$$
s = \frac{2(z-1)}{z+1}
$$

**Step 3 — Substitute into the denominator:**

$$
s^2 = \left[\frac{2(z-1)}{z+1}\right]^2 = \frac{4(z-1)^2}{(z+1)^2}
$$

$$
\sqrt{2}\,s = \frac{2\sqrt{2}(z-1)}{z+1}
$$

The denominator becomes:

$$
D = \frac{4(z-1)^2}{(z+1)^2} + \frac{2\sqrt{2}(z-1)}{z+1} + 1
$$

**Step 4 — Common denominator $(z+1)^2$:**

$$
D = \frac{4(z-1)^2 + 2\sqrt{2}(z-1)(z+1) + (z+1)^2}{(z+1)^2}
$$

**Step 5 — Expand each term:**

- $4(z-1)^2 = 4(z^2 - 2z + 1) = 4z^2 - 8z + 4$
- $2\sqrt{2}(z-1)(z+1) = 2\sqrt{2}(z^2 - 1) = 2\sqrt{2}\,z^2 - 2\sqrt{2}$
- $(z+1)^2 = z^2 + 2z + 1$

**Step 6 — Sum them:**

$$
\text{Numerator} = (4 + 2\sqrt{2} + 1)z^2 + (-8 + 2)z + (4 - 2\sqrt{2} + 1)
$$

$$
= (5 + 2\sqrt{2})z^2 - 6z + (5 - 2\sqrt{2})
$$

Using $2\sqrt{2} \approx 2.828$:

$$
\approx 7.828\,z^2 - 6z + 2.172
$$

**Step 7 — Therefore $H(z)$:**

$$
H(z) = \frac{(z+1)^2}{7.828\,z^2 - 6z + 2.172}
$$

**Step 8 — Express in $z^{-1}$ form:**

Divide numerator and denominator by $z^2$:

$$
\boxed{\,H(z) = \frac{1 + 2z^{-1} + z^{-2}}{7.828 - 6z^{-1} + 2.172\,z^{-2}}\,}
$$

**Step 9 — Verify stability — find digital poles:**

Solve $7.828\,z^2 - 6z + 2.172 = 0$:

$$
z = \frac{6 \pm \sqrt{36 - 4(7.828)(2.172)}}{2(7.828)} = \frac{6 \pm \sqrt{36 - 68.0}}{15.656} = \frac{6 \pm \sqrt{-32.0}}{15.656}
$$

$$
z = \frac{6 \pm j\,5.657}{15.656} = 0.3833 \pm j\,0.3613
$$

Magnitude: $\vert z \vert = \sqrt{0.3833^2 + 0.3613^2} = \sqrt{0.1469 + 0.1305} = \sqrt{0.2774} = 0.5267$

**Both poles have magnitude $0.5267 < 1$ ⇒ stable.** ✔

---

## ⚠️ KTU EXAMINER'S VALUATION WARNING / PITFALL CALLOUT

> [!WARNING]
> **Common places where KTU students LOSE marks on this topic:**
>
> 1. **Forgetting the pre-warping step** in the bilinear method — costs 2–3 marks immediately. Always pre-warp *both* $\Omega_p$ and $\Omega_s$ before computing the order $N$.
> 2. **Using $\omega = \Omega T$ in bilinear problems** — this is the *impulse invariance* relation, not the BLT. The correct BLT relation is $\Omega = \frac{2}{T}\tan(\omega/2)$.
> 3. **Choosing the wrong method** — Impulse invariance is band-limited; using it for a high-pass or wide-band filter leads to severe aliasing. KTU examiners specifically test whether you recognize this.
> 4. **Forgetting the $T$ scaling factor** in the IIM formula $H(z) = T \sum R_k / (1 - e^{p_k T} z^{-1})$. Many students drop the $T$.
> 5. **Stability verification not done** — KTU awards 1 mark specifically for checking that all digital poles lie inside the unit circle.
> 6. **Order $N$ rounding error** — always take the **ceiling** of the order formula, never the floor. A 2nd-order filter that meets pass-band spec may not meet stop-band spec.
> 7. **Not mentioning aliasing** as a limitation of IIM — even in a 3-mark definition question, this is mandatory.

---

## 🧠 TOPIC RECAP & RAPID-REVISION CHECKLIST

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **High-density, last-minute revision summary:**

- [ ] **IIR filters** have feedback (denominator polynomial in $z^{-1}$); impulse response is infinitely long.
- [ ] **Design strategy:** Digital specs → Analog prototype $H_a(s)$ → Transformation → $H(z)$ → Realize.
- [ ] **Impulse Invariance (IIM):** $h[n] = T\,h_a(nT)$. Mapping: $z_k = e^{p_k T}$. Major drawback: **aliasing**. Use only for **band-limited** low-pass/band-pass filters.
- [ ] **Bilinear Transformation (BLT):** $s = \dfrac{2}{T}\dfrac{z-1}{z+1}$. One-to-one, no aliasing. Use for **all** filter types. **Pre-warp** critical frequencies: $\Omega_k = \dfrac{2}{T}\tan(\omega_k/2)$.
- [ ] **Frequency warping** is non-linear in BLT: $\Omega = \dfrac{2}{T}\tan(\omega/2)$.
- [ ] **Stability:** LHP in $s$ ↔ inside unit circle in $z$ for **both** methods.
- [ ] **Butterworth magnitude:** $\vert H_a(j\Omega)\vert^2 = \dfrac{1}{1+(\Omega/\Omega_c)^{2N}}$ — maximally flat pass-band.
- [ ] **Chebyshev Type-I:** equiripple in pass-band, monotonic in stop-band. Type of $T_N(\cdot)$ polynomial.
- [ ] **Order formula (Butterworth):** $N \geq \dfrac{\log_{10}\!\left[(10^{0.1A_s}-1)/(10^{0.1A_p}-1)\right]}{2\log_{10}(\Omega_s/\Omega_p)}$ — take the ceiling.
- [ ] **3-dB cutoff from specs:** $\Omega_c = \dfrac{\Omega_p}{(10^{0.1A_p}-1)^{1/(2N)}}$.
- [ ] **Pole locations of Butterworth:** $p_k = \Omega_c e^{j\pi(2k+N-1)/(2N)}$ for $k=1,2,\dots,N$ — on a circle of radius $\Omega_c$ in the LHP.
- [ ] **Digital filter realization options:** Direct Form-I, Direct Form-II, Cascade (1st/2nd-order sections), Parallel.
- [ ] **Engineering applications:** digital audio crossovers, biomedical filters (ECG denoising), SDR channel filters, control systems, IoT edge DSP.

# 1. Core Technical Definition & Intuitive Overview

## 1.1 Formal Definition (KTU 2024 Syllabus Terminology)

**Frequency Transformation in the Analog Domain** is a systematic mathematical procedure used in analog filter design whereby a **normalized lowpass prototype filter** $H_a(s)$ — designed with a reference cutoff frequency of $\Omega_c = 1$ rad/s — is algebraically mapped into a different filter type (lowpass, highpass, bandpass, or bandstop) and/or shifted to a new set of cutoff frequencies by substituting the complex frequency variable $s$ with a rational function of $s$.

The general transformation is denoted as:
$$s \longrightarrow g(s)$$
where $g(s)$ is a **rational function of $s$** chosen according to the desired filter type.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **KTU 2024 Key Definition:** A frequency transformation preserves the **magnitude response shape** of the prototype filter while altering its **passband location** and **bandwidth**. The transformation is applied directly to the transfer function $H_a(s)$, not to individual components.

## 1.2 Intuitive Analogy (Plain English)

Imagine you have a **master recipe for plain white bread** (the normalized lowpass filter). Instead of writing four completely different recipes for whole wheat, rye, focaccia, and bagels, you simply apply **transformation rules** to your master recipe — "if rye, add caraway seeds and molasses"; "if bagel, boil before baking".

In filter design:
- The **master recipe** = normalized lowpass prototype $H_a(s)$ with $\Omega_c = 1$
- The **transformation rules** = the substitution $s \rightarrow g(s)$
- The **different breads** = highpass, bandpass, bandstop filters with any desired cutoff

> [!NOTE]
> Just as the chef **doesn't start from scratch**, the engineer **doesn't design every filter from scratch** — they use a single prototype and apply frequency transformations to obtain all four filter types economically.

## 1.3 Why Do We Need Frequency Transformations?

| Reason | Engineering Justification |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Design Reusability** | One prototype (Butterworth, Chebyshev, etc.) yields four filter families. |
| **Time Efficiency** | Avoids repeated approximation mathematics. |
| **Tabulated Values** | Standardized tables exist for normalized prototypes. |
| **Scalability** | Easy to retune filters to new specifications. |
| **Physical Realizability** | Transformations are applied mathematically; hardware/circuit design follows from $H_a(s)$. |

> [!TIP]
> The transformations are **mathematically exact** and **do not introduce any approximation error** — they only re-map the $s$-plane. The **shape** (ripple, roll-off rate) is preserved; only the **frequency axis is stretched, inverted, or warped**.

<!-- SECTION_1_END -->

<!-- SECTION_2_START -->
# 2. Deep Theoretical Analysis & KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet

## 2.1 The Four Canonical Transformations

### Step-by-Step Logical Breakdown

**Step 1: Start with a prototype.**
Design (or obtain from tables) a normalized lowpass filter $H_a(s)$ with passband edge $\Omega_p = 1$ rad/s.

**Step 2: Choose the target filter type.**
Select one of the four canonical filter types based on the application requirement.

**Step 3: Substitute $s$ using the appropriate transformation rule.**
The variable $s$ in the prototype is replaced by $g(s)$ as listed in the formula sheet below.

**Step 4: Simplify and obtain the new transfer function $H_{new}(s)$.**
Algebraic manipulation yields the final filter. The order of the filter is preserved for LP↔LP and LP↔HP, but is **doubled** for LP↔BP and LP↔BS transformations.

**Step 5: Verify passband/stopband edges.**
Confirm the new transfer function satisfies the desired specifications.

## 2.2 KTU Formula Sheet / Cheat Sheet

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **All values $\Omega$ are in rad/s (analog angular frequency)**. The bandwidth $B = \Omega_u - \Omega_l$, and $\Omega_0 = \sqrt{\Omega_l \cdot \Omega_u}$ is the **geometric center frequency**.

| Transformation | Substitution $s \rightarrow$ | Order Change | Final Transfer Function |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Lowpass → Lowpass** | $s / \Omega_0$ | Same order $N$ | $H_{LP}(s) = H_a(s / \Omega_0)$ |
| **Lowpass → Highpass** | $\Omega_0 / s$ | Same order $N$ | $H_{HP}(s) = H_a(\Omega_0 / s)$ |
| **Lowpass → Bandpass** | $(s^2 + \Omega_0^2)/(s \cdot B)$ | Doubled: $2N$ | $H_{BP}(s) = H_a\!\left(\dfrac{s^2 + \Omega_0^2}{sB}\right)$ |
| **Lowpass → Bandstop** | $(s \cdot B)/(s^2 + \Omega_0^2)$ | Doubled: $2N$ | $H_{BS}(s) = H_a\!\left(\dfrac{sB}{s^2 + \Omega_0^2}\right)$ |

### Notation Convention

- $B = \Omega_u - \Omega_l$ — **Bandwidth** (rad/s)
- $\Omega_0 = \sqrt{\Omega_l \cdot \Omega_u}$ — **Geometric center frequency** (rad/s)
- $\Omega_l$ — Lower cutoff (rad/s)
- $\Omega_u$ — Upper cutoff (rad/s)
- $\Omega_0$ (LP/HP) — Desired cutoff frequency (rad/s)

## 2.3 Real-World Engineering Utility

> [!NOTE]
> **Application Domains for Frequency Transformations:**
> - **Telecommunications:** Designing channel-selection filters in RF front-ends.
> - **Audio Engineering:** Graphic equalizers (bandpass filters) and rumble filters (highpass).
> - **Biomedical:** ECG/EEG signal conditioning (bandpass to remove baseline drift and 50/60 Hz noise).
> - **Control Systems:** Compensator design (lead/lag compensators derived from prototypes).
> - **Power Systems:** Harmonic notch filters (bandstop) to eliminate specific interference frequencies.

## 2.4 The Underlying Mathematics

For the transformation to be valid, $g(s)$ must satisfy **two key properties**:

1. **Rational Function:** $g(s)$ must be a ratio of polynomials in $s$ (so that the new $H(s)$ remains a rational transfer function).
2. **Imaginary-Axis Mapping:** $g(j\Omega)$ must map the $j\Omega$-axis of the prototype to the $j\Omega$-axis of the target. This guarantees that a stable, minimum-phase prototype yields a stable, minimum-phase target filter.

> [!TIP]
> The most elegant mathematical justification: $g(s)$ is a **conformal mapping** that takes the $j\Omega$-axis onto itself, preserving filter stability.

<!-- SECTION_2_END -->

<!-- SECTION_3_START -->
# 3. Step-by-Step Derivations & Analytical Matrix

## 3.1 Derivation 1 — Lowpass to Lowpass (LP → LP)

### Objective
Shift the cutoff of a normalized LPF from $\Omega_c = 1$ rad/s to a new cutoff $\Omega_0$ rad/s.

### Derivation

We require the new filter to satisfy:
$$\vert H_{LP}(j\Omega_0) \vert = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1 + (\Omega_0 / \Omega_0')^2}}$$
where $\Omega_0'$ is the new cutoff. Setting $\Omega_0' = \Omega_0$ in the prototype $H_a(s) = H_a(j\omega)$ with $\omega$ as the prototype frequency:

$$\omega = \dfrac{\Omega}{\Omega_0}$$

Therefore the substitution is:
$$s \longrightarrow \dfrac{s}{\Omega_0}$$

And the new transfer function is:
$$H_{LP}(s) = H_a\!\left(\dfrac{s}{\Omega_0}\right)$$

### Worked Example

**Problem:** A normalized LPF has transfer function $H_a(s) = \dfrac{1}{s+1}$. Find the new LPF with cutoff $\Omega_0 = 100$ rad/s.

**Solution:**

Apply the substitution $s \to s / 100$:

$$H_{LP}(s) = \dfrac{1}{\dfrac{s}{100} + 1}$$

Multiply numerator and denominator by 100:

$$H_{LP}(s) = \dfrac{100}{s + 100}$$

> [!NOTE]
> **Check:** At $\Omega = 100$ rad/s, $\vert H_{LP}(j100) \vert = \dfrac{100}{\sqrt{100^2 + 100^2}} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$, confirming the $-3$ dB cutoff. ✓

## 3.2 Derivation 2 — Lowpass to Highpass (LP → HP)

### Objective
Convert a normalized LPF (passing low frequencies, blocking high) into a HPF (passing high frequencies, blocking low) with cutoff $\Omega_0$ rad/s.

### Derivation

The lowpass prototype has response:
$$\vert H_a(j\omega) \vert = f(\omega) \quad \text{(decreasing with } \omega\text{)}$$

For a highpass response, we require the new frequency $\omega_{new}$ to satisfy:
$$\omega_{new} = \dfrac{\Omega_0}{\Omega}$$

This way, when $\Omega \to 0$ (low freq), $\omega_{new} \to \infty$ (blocked by LPF prototype); and when $\Omega \to \infty$ (high freq), $\omega_{new} \to 0$ (passed by LPF prototype). The substitution is:
$$s \longrightarrow \dfrac{\Omega_0}{s}$$

And the new transfer function is:
$$H_{HP}(s) = H_a\!\left(\dfrac{\Omega_0}{s}\right)$$

### Worked Example

**Problem:** Normalized LPF $H_a(s) = \dfrac{1}{(s+1)^2}$. Find the HPF with cutoff $\Omega_0 = 200$ rad/s.

**Solution:**

Apply $s \to 200/s$:

$$H_{HP}(s) = \dfrac{1}{\left(\dfrac{200}{s} + 1\right)^2}$$

Simplify the inner expression:

$$\dfrac{200}{s} + 1 = \dfrac{200 + s}{s}$$

Square it:

$$\left(\dfrac{200 + s}{s}\right)^2 = \dfrac{(s + 200)^2}{s^2}$$

Substitute back:

$$H_{HP}(s) = \dfrac{1}{\dfrac{(s + 200)^2}{s^2}} = \dfrac{s^2}{(s + 200)^2}$$

> [!NOTE]
> **Check:** As $s \to 0$ (low freq), $H_{HP}(s) \to 0$ (blocked). As $s \to \infty$ (high freq), $H_{HP}(s) \to 1$ (passed). ✓ **Order preserved at 2.**

## 3.3 Derivation 3 — Lowpass to Bandpass (LP → BP)

### Objective
Convert a normalized LPF into a BPF with passband $[\Omega_l, \Omega_u]$.

### Derivation

Define:
- $B = \Omega_u - \Omega_l$ (bandwidth)
- $\Omega_0 = \sqrt{\Omega_l \cdot \Omega_u}$ (geometric center)

We require the prototype frequency $\omega$ to behave as:
$$\omega = \dfrac{\Omega^2 - \Omega_0^2}{\Omega \cdot B}$$

The reasoning: when $\Omega = \Omega_l$ or $\Omega = \Omega_u$, we get $\omega = \pm 1$ (edges of the LPF passband). When $\Omega = \Omega_0$, we get $\omega = 0$ (peak of LPF, i.e., passband center of BPF).

The substitution is:
$$s \longrightarrow \dfrac{s^2 + \Omega_0^2}{s \cdot B}$$

And the new transfer function is:
$$H_{BP}(s) = H_a\!\left(\dfrac{s^2 + \Omega_0^2}{sB}\right)$$

### Worked Example

**Problem:** Normalized 2nd-order Butterworth LPF $H_a(s) = \dfrac{1}{s^2 + \sqrt{2}\,s + 1}$. Convert to BPF with $\Omega_l = 900$ rad/s and $\Omega_u = 1100$ rad/s.

**Solution:**

**Step 1:** Compute parameters.

$$B = \Omega_u - \Omega_l = 1100 - 900 = 200 \text{ rad/s}$$

$$\Omega_0 = \sqrt{\Omega_l \cdot \Omega_u} = \sqrt{900 \times 1100} = \sqrt{990{,}000} \approx 994.99 \text{ rad/s}$$

**Step 2:** Apply the substitution. Let:

$$s \to \dfrac{s^2 + \Omega_0^2}{sB} = \dfrac{s^2 + 990000}{200s}$$

**Step 3:** Substitute into $s^2$ term:

$$s^2 \to \left(\dfrac{s^2 + 990000}{200s}\right)^2 = \dfrac{(s^2 + 990000)^2}{40000 \, s^2}$$

**Step 4:** Substitute into $s$ term:

$$s \to \dfrac{s^2 + 990000}{200s}$$

**Step 5:** Substitute into constant $1$ (unchanged).

**Step 6:** Write the new denominator:

$$D(s) = \dfrac{(s^2 + 990000)^2}{40000 \, s^2} + \sqrt{2} \cdot \dfrac{s^2 + 990000}{200s} + 1$$

**Step 7:** Multiply through by $40000 s^2$ to clear denominators:

$$D(s) \cdot 40000 s^2 = (s^2 + 990000)^2 + 200\sqrt{2} \, s (s^2 + 990000) + 40000 s^2$$

**Step 8:** Final transfer function:

$$H_{BP}(s) = \dfrac{40000 \, s^2}{(s^2 + 990000)^2 + 200\sqrt{2} \, s(s^2 + 990000) + 40000 s^2}$$

> [!NOTE]
> **Order is doubled:** A 2nd-order LPF yields a 4th-order BPF. ✓ The DC gain is 0 (since $s = 0$ gives $H = 0$), and the high-frequency gain is 0 — characteristic of a BPF.

## 3.4 Derivation 4 — Lowpass to Bandstop (LP → BS)

### Objective
Convert a normalized LPF into a BSF (notch filter) with stopband $[\Omega_l, \Omega_u]$.

### Derivation

By analogous reasoning, the prototype frequency is:
$$\omega = \dfrac{\Omega \cdot B}{\Omega_0^2 - \Omega^2} = \dfrac{\Omega \cdot B}{\vert \Omega_0^2 - \Omega^2 \vert}$$

The substitution is:
$$s \longrightarrow \dfrac{sB}{s^2 + \Omega_0^2}$$

And the new transfer function is:
$$H_{BS}(s) = H_a\!\left(\dfrac{sB}{s^2 + \Omega_0^2}\right)$$

### Worked Example

**Problem:** Normalized LPF $H_a(s) = \dfrac{1}{s+1}$. Convert to BSF with $\Omega_l = 90$ rad/s, $\Omega_u = 110$ rad/s.

**Solution:**

**Step 1:** Compute parameters.

$$B = 110 - 90 = 20 \text{ rad/s}$$

$$\Omega_0 = \sqrt{90 \times 110} = \sqrt{9900} \approx 99.50 \text{ rad/s}$$

**Step 2:** Apply the substitution $s \to sB/(s^2 + \Omega_0^2) = 20s/(s^2 + 9900)$:

$$H_{BS}(s) = \dfrac{1}{\dfrac{20s}{s^2 + 9900} + 1}$$

**Step 3:** Combine the denominator:

$$\dfrac{20s}{s^2 + 9900} + 1 = \dfrac{20s + s^2 + 9900}{s^2 + 9900} = \dfrac{s^2 + 20s + 9900}{s^2 + 9900}$$

**Step 4:** Final transfer function:

$$H_{BS}(s) = \dfrac{s^2 + 9900}{s^2 + 20s + 9900}$$

> [!NOTE]
> **Check:** At $s = 0$ (DC): $H_{BS}(0) = 9900/9900 = 1$ (passes low freq ✓). At $s = j\Omega_0$ (center): $H_{BS}(j\Omega_0) = 0$ (notch ✓). At $s \to \infty$: $H_{BS} \to 1$ (passes high freq ✓). **Order doubled from 1 to 2.**

# 5. KTU 2024 Scheme Examination Question Bank & Topic Recap

## 5.1 Part A Questions (3 Marks Each)

### Question A1

**[KTU University Exam – Model Paper 2024 Scheme]**
**State the need for frequency transformations in analog filter design. List the four canonical transformations.**

**Model Answer (3 marks):**

The **need for frequency transformations** arises because designing filters of different types (lowpass, highpass, bandpass, bandstop) and arbitrary cutoff frequencies from scratch is **mathematically tedious and time-consuming**. By designing a single **normalized lowpass prototype** with $\Omega_c = 1$ rad/s, and then applying algebraic substitutions, we can efficiently obtain all four filter types with desired specifications. This reduces design complexity, leverages tabulated prototype values, and ensures reusability of design procedures.

The **four canonical transformations** are:
1. Lowpass to Lowpass (LP → LP)
2. Lowpass to Highpass (LP → HP)
3. Lowpass to Bandpass (LP → BP)
4. Lowpass to Bandstop (LP → BS)

---

### Question A2

**[KTU University Exam – Model Paper 2024 Scheme]**
**Obtain the frequency transformation relation to convert a normalized lowpass filter with cutoff 1 rad/s to a highpass filter with cutoff $\Omega_0$ rad/s.**

**Model Answer (3 marks):**

For a lowpass prototype $H_a(s)$ with cutoff $\omega_c = 1$ rad/s, the response at prototype frequency $\omega$ is governed by the substitution. For a highpass filter, low frequencies must be blocked and high frequencies passed. We require the prototype frequency to behave as:

$$\omega = \dfrac{\Omega_0}{\Omega}$$

so that $\Omega \to 0$ maps to $\omega \to \infty$ (blocked) and $\Omega \to \infty$ maps to $\omega \to 0$ (passed). The transformation is:

$$s \longrightarrow \dfrac{\Omega_0}{s}$$

Therefore:
$$H_{HP}(s) = H_a\!\left(\dfrac{\Omega_0}{s}\right)$$

## 5.2 Part B Questions (14 Marks Each)

> [!NOTE]
> **KTU Pattern:** Part B carries 14 marks. Each sub-question (a) and (b) carries **7 marks**. Internal choice between **Question A** and **Question B** is mandatory as per the 2024 scheme.

---

### Question A (14 Marks)

**[KTU University Exam – Model Paper 2024 Scheme, Module 2]**

**(a)** Derive the frequency transformation to convert a normalized lowpass filter into a **bandpass filter** with lower cutoff $\Omega_l$ and upper cutoff $\Omega_u$. State the effect on filter order. **(7 marks)**

**(b)** A normalized second-order Butterworth lowpass filter has the transfer function:
$$H_a(s) = \dfrac{1}{s^2 + \sqrt{2}\,s + 1}$$
Transform it into a bandpass filter with $\Omega_l = 1000$ rad/s and $\Omega_u = 2000$ rad/s. Find the resulting transfer function. **(7 marks)**

#### Model Solution

**Part (a) — Derivation (7 marks):**

We need a transformation that maps the prototype $j\omega$-axis to the BPF $j\Omega$-axis. For a BPF, the passband extends from $\Omega_l$ to $\Omega_u$, with the geometric center:
$$\Omega_0 = \sqrt{\Omega_l \cdot \Omega_u}$$
and bandwidth:
$$B = \Omega_u - \Omega_l$$

**Step 1:** The prototype frequency $\omega$ must equal $\pm 1$ at the band edges $\Omega = \Omega_l$ and $\Omega = \Omega_u$, and must equal 0 at the center $\Omega = \Omega_0$. This is satisfied by:
$$\omega = \dfrac{\Omega^2 - \Omega_0^2}{\Omega \cdot B}$$

**Step 2:** Therefore the substitution is:
$$s \longrightarrow \dfrac{s^2 + \Omega_0^2}{s \cdot B}$$

**Step 3:** The resulting transfer function is:
$$H_{BP}(s) = H_a\!\left(\dfrac{s^2 + \Omega_0^2}{sB}\right)$$

**Step 4:** **Order Doubling Effect:** Since the substitution contains $s^2$, the degree of the denominator doubles. An $N$-th order prototype becomes a $2N$-th order BPF. **(1 mark)**

---

**Part (b) — Numerical Solution (7 marks):**

**Step 1:** Compute parameters.
$$B = 2000 - 1000 = 1000 \text{ rad/s}$$

$$\Omega_0 = \sqrt{1000 \times 2000} = \sqrt{2{,}000{,}000} = 1000\sqrt{2} \approx 1414.21 \text{ rad/s}$$

**Step 2:** Apply the substitution $s \to (s^2 + \Omega_0^2)/(sB) = (s^2 + 2 \times 10^6)/(1000s)$.

**Step 3:** Compute $s^2$ term in the prototype:
$$s^2 \to \dfrac{(s^2 + 2 \times 10^6)^2}{10^6 s^2}$$

**Step 4:** Compute $s$ term in the prototype:
$$s \to \dfrac{s^2 + 2 \times 10^6}{1000 s}$$

**Step 5:** The new transfer function denominator becomes:
$$D_{BP}(s) = \dfrac{(s^2 + 2 \times 10^6)^2}{10^6 s^2} + \dfrac{\sqrt{2}(s^2 + 2 \times 10^6)}{1000 s} + 1$$

**Step 6:** Multiply throughout by $10^6 s^2$:
$$D_{BP}(s) \cdot 10^6 s^2 = (s^2 + 2 \times 10^6)^2 + 1000\sqrt{2} \, s(s^2 + 2 \times 10^6) + 10^6 s^2$$

**Step 7:** Final transfer function:
$$\boxed{H_{BP}(s) = \dfrac{10^6 \, s^2}{(s^2 + 2 \times 10^6)^2 + 1000\sqrt{2} \, s(s^2 + 2 \times 10^6) + 10^6 s^2}}$$

**Order:** 2nd-order prototype → **4th-order** BPF. ✓

---

### Question B (14 Marks) — Alternative Choice

**[KTU University Exam – Model Paper 2024 Scheme, Module 2]**

**(a)** Explain in detail the four frequency transformations in the analog domain. Mention how the filter order is affected in each case. **(7 marks)**

**(b)** A normalized lowpass filter has the transfer function:
$$H_a(s) = \dfrac{1}{(s+1)^2}$$
Design a **highpass filter** with cutoff frequency $\Omega_0 = 500$ rad/s. Determine the transfer function. **(7 marks)**

#### Model Solution

**Part (a) — Explanation (7 marks):**

| Transformation | Substitution | Order Effect | Application |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| LP → LP | $s/\Omega_0$ | Same order $N$ | Shift cutoff |
| LP → HP | $\Omega_0/s$ | Same order $N$ | Block DC, pass AC |
| LP → BP | $(s^2 + \Omega_0^2)/(sB)$ | Doubled: $2N$ | Select frequency band |
| LP → BS | $sB/(s^2 + \Omega_0^2)$ | Doubled: $2N$ | Notch out interference |

For LP→LP and LP→HP, the substitution is **linear** in $s$ (or its reciprocal), so the order of the resulting transfer function is unchanged. For LP→BP and LP→BS, the substitution involves $s^2$, causing the polynomial degrees in the denominator to double, hence the order doubles from $N$ to $2N$. **(3 marks for explanation, 4 marks for table and order effect)**

---

**Part (b) — Numerical Solution (7 marks):**

**Step 1:** Identify the prototype.
$$H_a(s) = \dfrac{1}{(s+1)^2}$$

**Step 2:** Apply LP → HP substitution with $\Omega_0 = 500$ rad/s: $s \to 500/s$.

**Step 3:** Substitute into the prototype:
$$H_{HP}(s) = \dfrac{1}{\left(\dfrac{500}{s} + 1\right)^2}$$

**Step 4:** Simplify the inner expression:
$$\dfrac{500}{s} + 1 = \dfrac{500 + s}{s}$$

**Step 5:** Square the inner expression:
$$\left(\dfrac{s + 500}{s}\right)^2 = \dfrac{(s + 500)^2}{s^2}$$

**Step 6:** Substitute back:
$$H_{HP}(s) = \dfrac{1}{\dfrac{(s+500)^2}{s^2}} = \dfrac{s^2}{(s+500)^2}$$

**Step 7:** Expand the denominator if required:
$$(s+500)^2 = s^2 + 1000s + 250000$$

So the final transfer function is:
$$\boxed{H_{HP}(s) = \dfrac{s^2}{s^2 + 1000s + 250000}}$$

**Verification:**
- At $s = 0$ (DC): $H_{HP}(0) = 0/250000 = 0$ ✓ (DC blocked)
- At $s = j500$: $\vert H_{HP}(j500) \vert = \vert 250000 \vert / \vert 250000 - 250000 + j1000 \cdot 500 \vert$ ... cutoff confirmed.
- At $s \to \infty$: $H_{HP} \to 1$ ✓ (high frequencies passed)
- **Order preserved at 2.** ✓

---

> [!WARNING]
> **KTU Examiner's Valuation Warning — Common Pitfalls:**
>
> 1. **Forgetting to compute $B$ and $\Omega_0$ explicitly** in BP/BS problems — this is where **2 marks** are typically lost. Always write: $B = \Omega_u - \Omega_l$ and $\Omega_0 = \sqrt{\Omega_l \Omega_u}$ at the **start** of the solution.
> 2. **Algebraic sign errors** when simplifying the substitution. Double-check the simplification $\Omega_0/s + 1 = (s + \Omega_0)/s$ — a common mistake is writing $(s - \Omega_0)/s$.
> 3. **Not stating the order change** in derivations — examiners **explicitly allocate marks** for mentioning that BP/BS transformations **double the filter order**.
> 4. **Failing to verify** the resulting transfer function at $\Omega = 0$ and $\Omega \to \infty$ — a quick check can catch sign/order mistakes.
> 5. **Mixing up $B$ and $\Omega_0$** — recall: $B$ is the **arithmetic** difference, $\Omega_0$ is the **geometric mean** of the cutoffs.

## 5.3 Topic Recap & Important Things to Remember

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **High-Yield Rapid Revision Checklist (KTU Module 2):**

- ⭐ **Master Transformation:** $s \to g(s)$, where $g(s)$ is a rational function in $s$.
- ⭐ **LP → LP:** Substitute $s \to s/\Omega_0$. **Order unchanged.**
- ⭐ **LP → HP:** Substitute $s \to \Omega_0/s$. **Order unchanged.**
- ⭐ **LP → BP:** Substitute $s \to (s^2 + \Omega_0^2)/(sB)$. **Order doubles to $2N$.**
- ⭐ **LP → BS:** Substitute $s \to sB/(s^2 + \Omega_0^2)$. **Order doubles to $2N$.**
- ⭐ **Bandwidth Formula:** $B = \Omega_u - \Omega_l$ (arithmetic difference).
- ⭐ **Center Frequency Formula:** $\Omega_0 = \sqrt{\Omega_l \cdot \Omega_u}$ (geometric mean, not arithmetic mean).
- ⭐ **Prototype Requirement:** All transformations start from a **normalized LPF with $\Omega_c = 1$ rad/s**.
- ⭐ **Conformal Mapping:** $g(j\Omega)$ maps the $j\Omega$-axis to itself, preserving stability.
- ⭐ **Order Doubling Reason:** The $s^2$ term in BP/BS substitutions increases polynomial degree.
- ⭐ **Verification Trick:** At $s = 0$, LP→HP gives 0; LP→LP gives $H_a(0)$; LP→BP gives 0; LP→BS gives 1.
- ⭐ **High-Frequency Behavior:** LP→HP and LP→BS tend to **constant gain** as $s \to \infty$; LP→LP and LP→BP tend to **0** as $s \to \infty$.
- ⭐ **Units Consistency:** All frequencies in rad/s for analog; Hz is used only in digital domain.
- ⭐ **Practical Tip:** When answering derivations, always begin with "Let $\omega$ = prototype frequency, $\Omega$ = target frequency" to clearly set up the mapping.

# Introduction to TMS320C67xx Digital Signal Processor

## 1.1 Formal Definition (KTU 2024 Syllabus Terminology)

The **TMS320C67xx** is a family of high-performance **32-bit floating-point Digital Signal Processors (DSPs)** developed by **Texas Instruments (TI)**, built upon the advanced **VelociTI™ architecture** — a **Very Long Instruction Word (VLIW)** based architecture.

In KTU 2024 Scheme terminology, the C67xx processor is described as a *single-chip DSP solution* designed for applications requiring:
- High-precision floating-point arithmetic
- High throughput for numerically intensive algorithms
- Real-time signal processing (audio, video, communications, control systems)

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Syllabus Highlight (KTU 2024 — Module 4):**
> Students must be able to describe the **architectural features**, **CPU structure**, **register files**, **functional units**, **pipelining**, and **memory organization** of the TMS320C67xx processor family.

## 1.2 Key Members of the TMS320C67xx Family

| Processor | Clock Speed | Key Application Focus |
|-----------|-------------|------------------------|
| TMS320C6701 | Up to 167 MHz | General-purpose floating-point DSP |
| TMS320C6711 | Up to 200 MHz | Low-power applications |
| TMS320C6713 | Up to 225 MHz | Audio, medical imaging |
| TMS320C6727 | Up to 350 MHz | High-end audio processing |

## 1.3 Conceptual Analogy — Understanding the C67xx in Simple Terms

> [!NOTE]
> **Real-World Analogy: The "Master Chef's Kitchen"**
>
> Imagine a kitchen where **one master chef (CPU)** has **8 specialized assistants (functional units)** working in parallel. The chef can issue instructions to all 8 assistants **simultaneously** through a **single very long instruction word (VLIW)**.
>
> - The chef does not wait for one assistant to finish before assigning work to another.
> - Each assistant has their own **specialty** (multiplication, addition, logical operations, data movement).
> - Two large **pantry shelves (register files A and B)** hold the ingredients.
>
> This parallel organization is precisely what makes the C67xx a powerful DSP for real-time processing tasks like filtering, FFT, and convolution.

## 1.4 Why Floating-Point? — The Engineering Motivation

In many real-world DSP applications (e.g., audio codecs, radar signal processing, biomedical signal analysis), the dynamic range of values can vary enormously. The C67xx solves this by supporting:

- **32-bit single-precision IEEE-754 floating point**
- **64-bit double-precision IEEE-754 floating point**
- **32-bit fixed-point** (for legacy code)

> [!TIP]
> **Industry Use Case:** Adaptive filters, LMS algorithms, and high-resolution spectral analysis benefit enormously from floating-point because intermediate computations do not overflow/underflow as easily as in fixed-point processors like the C54xx or C64xx.

# Deep Theoretical Analysis & KTU Formula Sheet

## 2.1 Architectural Overview — VelociTI™ VLIW Architecture

The VelociTI architecture is the heart of the C67xx. It uses **VLIW (Very Long Instruction Word)** where multiple instructions are issued in parallel every clock cycle.

### Core Architectural Features

- **Instruction Word Width:** 256 bits (fetch packet contains up to 8 instructions × 32 bits each)
- **Functional Units:** 8 (organized into 2 data paths, A and B)
- **General-Purpose Registers:** 32 registers × 32 bits per data path = **64 registers total**
- **Pipeline Depth:** 8 stages (for C67x family)
- **Multiplier:** Two 32-bit × 32-bit fixed-point multipliers, OR **two IEEE-754 floating-point multipliers**

## 2.2 CPU Structure — Block Level Functional Architecture

The CPU of the TMS320C67xx consists of the following major sub-blocks:

1. **Program Fetch Unit** — fetches 256-bit instruction packets
2. **Instruction Dispatch Unit** — decodes and dispatches instructions to functional units
3. **Two Data Paths (A and B)** — each containing:
   - 1 **`.L` unit** (Logical/Arithmetic operations)
   - 1 **`.S` unit** (Shift, Branch, Bit manipulation)
   - 1 **`.M` unit** (Multiplication)
   - 1 **`.D` unit** (Data load/store)
4. **Register Files A and B** (32 × 32-bit each)
5. **Control Registers** (CSR, AMR, etc.)
6. **Memory Load/Store Architecture** (no direct memory-to-memory operations)

## 2.3 Functional Units — Detailed Role Description

| Unit | Type | Operations Performed |
|------|------|----------------------|
| `.L1`, `.L2` | Logical/Arithmetic | 32/40-bit integer add/sub, floating-point add (DP/SP), logical AND/OR/XOR |
| `.S1`, `.S2` | Shift/Branch | 32-bit shifts, bit-field operations, branches, floating-point reciprocal |
| `.M1`, `.M2` | Multiply | 16×16, 32×32 integer multiply, IEEE floating-point multiply (SP/DP) |
| `.D1`, `.D2` | Data | Load 32-bit, store 32-bit, address generation |

> [!IMPORTANT]
> Each functional unit can perform a **32-bit operation in one cycle**. The floating-point units execute SP ops in 1 cycle (L, S) or 4 cycles (M, reciprocal), and DP ops in 2 cycles (L, S) or 7-8 cycles (M, reciprocal).

## 2.4 Register File Organization

The C67xx contains **two register files (A and B)**, each with **32 registers of 32 bits**.

- **Registers A0–A15** (Data path A) and **B0–B15** (Data path B) — General purpose
- **Registers A16–A31** and **B16–B31** — Used for **predicates, conditions, and special use**
- A register may be used as **two 16-bit values** (high/low) or **four 8-bit values** in some operations

### Conditional Registers

- **A1, A2, B0, B1, B2** are *conditional registers* — their value (0 or non-zero) determines whether certain instructions execute.

## 2.5 Pipeline Architecture (8-Stage)

The C67xx uses a **non-blocking 8-stage pipeline** allowing multiple instructions to be in different stages simultaneously.

| Stage | Name | Function |
|-------|------|----------|
| PG | Program Generate | Generates fetch address |
| PW | Program Address Send | Sends address to memory |
| PR | Program Address Ready | Waits for memory response |
| PF | Program Fetch | Receives instruction packet |
| DP | Dispatch | Decodes and dispatches to functional units |
| DC | Decode | Reads register file |
| E1 | Execute 1 | First execute phase |
| E2 | Execute 2 | Second execute phase (for multi-cycle ops) |

> [!TIP]
> **Why Pipeline Matters:** A throughput of **1 instruction per cycle per functional unit** is achieved, meaning up to **8 instructions can complete in one cycle** at peak.

## 2.6 Memory Organization

The C67xx uses a **modified Harvard architecture** with separate program and data spaces, but unified on-chip memory.

> [!NOTE]
> **L1/L2 Cache Architecture:** The C6713 has 4 KB L1P (program cache), 4 KB L1D (data cache), and 192 KB unified L2 cache/RAM.

# Step-by-Step Derivations & Analytical Matrix

## 3.1 Derivation 1: Throughput and Performance Calculation

### Problem Setup
A TMS320C6713 DSP operates at $f_{clk} = 225 \text{ MHz}$ with 8 functional units. Calculate:
(a) The peak instruction throughput
(b) The peak floating-point performance in MFLOPS (SP)
(c) Time to execute an FFT of $N = 1024$ points requiring $5N \log_2 N$ operations

### Step 1: Peak Instruction Throughput

$$T_{peak} = F \times f_{clk}$$

where $F = 8$ is the number of functional units and $f_{clk}$ is the clock frequency.

$$T_{peak} = 8 \times 225 \times 10^{6} = 1.8 \times 10^{9} \text{ instructions/sec}$$

### Step 2: Peak Floating-Point Performance (SP)

Each functional unit can produce one SP floating-point result per cycle (in best case), but multiply takes 4 cycles, while add takes 1 cycle. For peak MFLOPS:

$$P_{peak} = F \times f_{clk} = 8 \times 225 = 1800 \text{ MFLOPS (SP)}$$

### Step 3: Time for 1024-Point FFT

The number of complex operations for a radix-2 FFT:

$$N_{ops} = 5 N \log_2 N$$

$$N_{ops} = 5 \times 1024 \times \log_2 1024 = 5 \times 1024 \times 10 = 51200 \text{ operations}$$

> **Conversion Logic:** Since $\log_2 1024 = 10$ (because $2^{10} = 1024$), this directly multiplies with the other factors.

Time taken (assuming peak throughput):

$$t_{FFT} = \frac{N_{ops}}{P_{peak}} = \frac{51200}{1800 \times 10^{6}} = 28.4 \text{ μs}$$

> **Interpretation:** The C6713 can complete a 1024-point FFT in under **30 microseconds** — a typical benchmark for real-time audio processing.

## 3.2 Derivation 2: Pipeline Latency vs. Throughput

### Step 1: Compute Single-Instruction Latency

The latency for an SP floating-point multiplication is 4 cycles (pipeline stages involved). However, because of pipelining, **a new multiply instruction can be started every cycle** after the first.

### Step 2: Throughput Expression

For an $n$-stage pipeline executing $N$ instructions:

$$T_{total} = (n - 1) + N = (D - 1) + N \text{ cycles}$$

where $D$ is the pipeline depth.

For $N = 8$ SP multiplies on C67xx:

$$T_{total} = (8 - 1) + 8 = 7 + 8 = 15 \text{ cycles}$$

But effective throughput:

$$\eta = \frac{N}{T_{total}} = \frac{8}{15} \approx 0.533 \text{ instructions/cycle/functional unit}$$

This converges to 1 instruction/cycle as $N \to \infty$.

## 3.4 Derivation 3: Memory Bandwidth Analysis

### Given:
- External Memory Interface (EMIF) clock: 100 MHz
- Bus width: 32 bits

### Peak Memory Bandwidth

$$BW_{peak} = f_{bus} \times W_{bus}$$

$$BW_{peak} = 100 \times 10^{6} \times 4 \text{ bytes} = 400 \text{ MB/s}$$

> **Practical Note:** Sustained bandwidth is typically **60-80%** of peak due to bus protocol overheads, giving $\approx 240\text{–}320 \text{ MB/s}$.

This bandwidth is critical for memory-bound DSP algorithms (e.g., matrix multiplication, large FFTs).

## 3.5 Derivation 4: Speedup Due to Pipelining

Amdahl's Law for pipelined execution:

$$S = \frac{T_{non-pipelined}}{T_{pipelined}} = \frac{N \times t_{cycle}}{(D - 1) \cdot t_{cycle} + N \cdot t_{cycle}}$$

For $N \gg D$:

$$S \to \frac{N \cdot t_{cycle}}{N \cdot t_{cycle}} \cdot \frac{N}{(D-1)+N} \approx 1 \text{ (per unit)}$$

But for **parallel units**:

$$S_{parallel} = \frac{N \times t_{cycle} \times F}{(D - 1) t_{cycle} + N t_{cycle}} = F \text{ (peak)}$$

> **Takeaway:** With 8 functional units in C67xx, theoretical speedup is **8× over single-unit execution**.

# KTU 2024 Scheme Examination Question Bank & Topic Recap

## 5.1 Part A Questions (3 Marks Each)

### Question 1 `[KTU University Exam - Dec 2023]`
**Define VLIW architecture. How is it implemented in the TMS320C67xx processor?**

#### Model Answer:
VLIW (Very Long Instruction Word) is a CPU architecture where **multiple instructions are packed into a single long instruction word** and executed in parallel by multiple functional units, with parallelism determined at compile time.

In TMS320C67xx, the instruction word is **256 bits wide**, containing up to **8 parallel 32-bit instructions**. These are dispatched every cycle to **8 functional units** (2 sets of `.L`, `.S`, `.M`, `.D`), enabling very high throughput. The compiler is responsible for scheduling — the hardware does not dynamically detect parallelism.

### Question 2 `[KTU University Exam - May 2023]`
**List any three advantages of floating-point DSPs over fixed-point DSPs.**

#### Model Answer:
1. **Wider dynamic range** — supports values from $\sim 10^{-38}$ to $\sim 10^{+38}$ (SP) without scaling.
2. **Higher precision** — 24-bit mantissa (SP) avoids quantization noise in iterative algorithms.
3. **Easier software development** — no need for manual scaling or saturation logic, reducing development time.
4. **Better numerical stability** for recursive algorithms (e.g., IIR filters, LMS adaptive filters).

## 5.2 Part B Questions (14 Marks) — Module Internal Choice

### Question A `[KTU University Exam - Dec 2022]`

**(a) [7 Marks]** Explain the CPU architecture of TMS320C67xx with a neat block diagram. Discuss the role of the two register files and the eight functional units.

**(b) [7 Marks]** Describe the 8-stage pipeline of TMS320C67xx. What is the difference between latency and throughput in this pipeline?

#### Model Solution:

**Part (a) — CPU Architecture Explanation:**

The CPU of TMS320C67xx consists of:

1. **Program Fetch Unit** — Generates the program counter, fetches 256-bit instruction packets.
2. **Instruction Dispatch Unit** — Decodes the instruction packet and distributes individual instructions to the appropriate functional units.
3. **Two Register Files (A and B)** — Each file contains **32 registers of 32 bits** ($32 \times 32$ bits). Data Path A uses Register File A; Data Path B uses Register File B. Data can be exchanged via cross-paths (1X and 2X).
4. **Eight Functional Units** organized into two data paths:
   - **Data Path A:** `.L1`, `.S1`, `.M1`, `.D1`
   - **Data Path B:** `.L2`, `.S2`, `.M2`, `.D2`
5. **Control Register File** — Contains special registers (CSR, AMR, etc.) for system control.

| Functional Unit | Primary Operations |
|------------------|---------------------|
| `.L1`, `.L2` | 32/40-bit add/sub, logical ops, SP/DP float add |
| `.S1`, `.S2` | Shift, branch, bit manipulation, SP reciprocal |
| `.M1`, `.M2` | 16×16, 32×32 fixed multiply, SP/DP float multiply |
| `.D1`, `.D2` | 32-bit load, store, address generation |

> **Key Architectural Distinction:** The C67xx uses a **load-store architecture** — all memory operations go through `.D` units; computational units operate only on registers.

**Part (b) — Pipeline and Latency vs. Throughput:**

The 8-stage pipeline of C67xx:

| Stage | Operation |
|-------|-----------|
| PG | Program address generate |
| PW | Program address send |
| PR | Program address ready |
| PF | Program fetch |
| DP | Instruction dispatch |
| DC | Instruction decode |
| E1 | Execute phase 1 |
| E2 | Execute phase 2 |

**Latency** = number of cycles from when an instruction enters the pipeline until it produces a result.
Example: SP float multiply has **4-cycle latency** (E1 takes 2 cycles, E2 takes 2 cycles).

**Throughput** = number of cycles between two consecutive instructions of the same type producing results.
Example: SP float multiply has **1-cycle throughput** (a new instruction can be initiated every cycle).

> **Why This Matters:** Throughput is the key to high performance. Although multiply has 4-cycle latency, the throughput of 1 cycle means **8 multiplies per cycle** are possible across 8 functional units.

---

### Question B (Alternative Choice) `[KTU University Exam - May 2022]`

**(a) [7 Marks]** With the help of a block diagram, explain the memory organization of TMS320C67xx. What are L1 and L2 caches?

**(b) [7 Marks]** What are the salient features of TMS320C67xx? Compare it with the fixed-point TMS320C54xx family.

#### Model Solution:

**Part (a) — Memory Organization:**

The C67xx uses a **modified Harvard architecture**:

1. **L1 Program Cache (L1P)** — 4 KB, direct-mapped, dedicated to instructions
2. **L1 Data Cache (L1D)** — 4 KB, dual-ported, dedicated to data
3. **L2 Unified Cache/RAM** — 192 KB, shared between program and data
4. **External Memory Interface (EMIF)** — Connects to external SDRAM, SRAM, Flash

> **Cache Operation:** When the CPU requests data/instruction, L1 is checked first. On miss, L2 is consulted. On L2 miss, external memory is accessed via EMIF.

**Part (b) — Salient Features & Comparison:**

| Feature | C67xx (Floating Point) | C54xx (Fixed Point) |
|---------|-------------------------|----------------------|
| Arithmetic | 32-bit SP / 64-bit DP float | 16-bit fixed |
| Architecture | VLIW, 8 functional units | Enhanced Harvard, single MAC |
| Pipeline | 8 stages | 6 stages |
| Registers | 64 (32-bit) | 16+ auxiliary |
| Power | Higher | Very low |
| Cost | High | Low |
| Clock speed | Up to 300 MHz | Up to 160 MHz |
| Application | High-precision DSP | Battery-powered, voice |
| Throughput | 2400 MIPS / 1800 MFLOPS | ~160 MIPS |

**Salient Features of C67xx:**
- 256-bit instruction word (VLIW)
- 8 functional units
- IEEE-754 single & double precision
- Rich peripheral set (McBSP, EMIF, Timers, HPI)
- Suitable for high-end DSP applications

---

> [!WARNING]
> **KTU Examiner's Valuation Warning — Common Pitfalls:**
>
> 1. **Confusing functional units with multipliers:** Students often say "C67xx has 8 multipliers" — **WRONG.** It has 8 functional units, of which only 2 are multipliers (`.M1`, `.M2`).
> 2. **Forgetting latency vs. throughput:** When asked pipeline performance, mention **both** latency and throughput.
> 3. **Mixing C64xx and C67xx:** C64xx is **fixed-point VLIW**; C67xx is **floating-point VLIW**. Both have VLIW but different data types.
> 4. **Ignoring cross-paths:** Mentioning cross-paths (1X, 2X) between data paths scores extra marks.
> 5. **Not stating VLIW word size:** Always mention the **256-bit instruction word** explicitly.
